The staff room of the Dharavi community learning centre was quiet after the evening batch left. Charu sat with three printed lesson plans and a timer.
The interview panel for the senior teacher post would watch her teach a demo class on Saturday. Yusuf, who ran the computer lab, looked in. “Still here? You'll be fine. Just wing it, like the rest of us.”
“If I wing it and fail, I'll never know what went wrong,” Charu said. “If I prepare properly and fail, at least they'll tell me something real.”
She taught the class to the empty chairs twice, timing each part. Her stomach fluttered at the thought of trying her hardest and still being turned down.
On Saturday she wasn't selected. The panel said her pacing was excellent but her questions were too closed.
Walking home, she felt disappointed, and oddly clear. She wrote one line in her diary: “Open questions. Practise.”

qa.q: What did the panel say about Charu's demo class?
qa.a: They said her pacing was excellent but her questions were too closed.

qa.q: How did Charu feel walking home?
qa.a: She felt disappointed but oddly clear, because full effort meant the result gave her real information.

qa.q: Why was Charu's choice not to wing it a good one?
qa.a: Preparing properly risked her pride, but it turned the rejection into useful feedback she can practise on.

qa.q: What would change if Charu had followed Yusuf's advice?
qa.a: A rejection would feel easier to explain away, but she would not have learned that her questions need to be more open.

grounding: The passage shows an adult choosing to prepare fully for a risky attempt and treating the poor result as information.

subtype: Trying fully and accepting the result [Response]
passage:
Dear Lakshmi Ma'am,

You once told our class that half-effort is a way of hiding. I think of it every time I apply for something.

This spring I entered the state furniture design competition. For years I'd entered things at the last minute and blamed the rush. This time I did the full process: sketches, a scale model, testing the joints, even asking a carpenter in my lane to break my prototype on purpose.

It was frightening. If I lost after all that, I couldn't blame the rush. It would just be the truth about my work.

I didn't win. I came sixth of forty. The judges wrote that my chair was strong but “visually timid.”

Strangely, I'm not crushed. I know exactly what to work on now. That feels better than any excuse ever did.

With thanks,
Jahnavi

qa.q: What place did Jahnavi come in the competition?
qa.a: Jahnavi came sixth of forty.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi find the full process frightening?
qa.a: Jahnavi was scared that losing after full effort would be the plain truth about the work, with no rush to blame.

qa.q: What did preparing properly give Jahnavi that excuses never did?
qa.a: A clear, usable comment, “visually timid,” that shows exactly what to work on next.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Ma'am feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Lakshmi Ma'am would probably feel proud and touched that an old lesson helped a former student grow.

grounding: The letter shows an adult preparing fully for a competition and accepting a poor result as useful information rather than hiding behind a rush.

subtype: Trying fully and accepting the result [Response]
passage:
So, Akash, you asked why I didn't just enter the open mic without rehearsing, like last year.
I'm Jasleen, and last year I went up with half a set scribbled on my hand. It bombed. And I said to everyone, “Well, I didn't prepare, so.” Very convenient.
This year I decided to actually try. I wrote twelve minutes of material. I performed it to my bathroom mirror, to my flatmate, to two friends in a café. I recorded myself and cringed.
The scary part was knowing that if it bombed this time, it was just me. No excuse.
It half-bombed. The first four minutes were great. The rest died.
But here's the thing: I know exactly which jokes died, and why. I've rewritten them. That's never happened before. Last year's excuse gave me nothing. This year's flop gave me a notebook full of fixes.

qa.q: How many minutes of material did Jasleen write this year?
qa.a: Jasleen wrote twelve minutes of material.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen find it scary to prepare fully this time?
qa.a: Jasleen felt nervous because a flop after real effort would have no excuse and would say something true about Jasleen's comedy.

qa.q: What did full effort give Jasleen that the excuse didn't?
qa.a: Specific knowledge of which jokes died and why, so they could be rewritten.

qa.q: How might Akash see Jasleen's two open mics?
qa.a: Akash might see that the second, though it half-bombed, helped Jasleen grow in a way the first never could.

grounding: The monologue shows an adult choosing full preparation for a risky performance and accepting a poor result as useful information.

passage:
In the coldest week of the Lohri holidays the power had gone. Irawati, five, sat by the window in two sweaters with three stubby crayons and an old calendar.
She drew a bonfire. Then a dog near the bonfire. Then a very long kite string going off the page.
Her cousin Lalremsiami peeked in and went away again. Irawati didn't look up.
The light outside turned grey. The blue crayon broke. She used the broken half.
After a long time she put the crayons down, nodded once at the page, and went to find a biscuit. She showed no one.

qa.q: What did Irawati draw first?
qa.a: She drew a bonfire.

qa.q: What does Irawati's nod at the end suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt satisfied and content that the drawing was finished, without needing anyone to praise it.

qa.q: How could an adult support this kind of play?
qa.a: By leaving her some paper and crayons and not interrupting or asking for a show, so drawing stays fun for its own sake.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami think on peeking in and seeing Irawati so absorbed?
qa.a: Lalremsiami might feel amused and decide not to disturb her, seeing she is happy on her own.

grounding: The passage shows a young child drawing for a long time in a cold power cut with no audience and stopping when she feels finished.

In the Durga Puja holidays, everyone went to the pandals each evening. Arnab, five, had a runny nose, so he stayed home with his big cousin Raghav.
Arnab spread a big sheet and all his sketch pens on the floor. He drew the goddess with ten arms. Then a lion. Then twenty more arms, because arms were fun to draw.
Raghav said, “Nice! Shall I send a photo to your mum?”
Arnab shook his head without looking up and kept drawing.
Faraway drums beat. Nearly an hour passed.
Then Arnab capped his pens one by one and said, “Done.” He left the drawing on the floor and went to find his toy car.

qa.q: What did Arnab draw after the lion?
qa.a: He drew twenty more arms, because arms were fun to draw.

qa.q: Why did Arnab shake his head when Raghav offered to send a photo?
qa.a: He felt content and absorbed and didn't need anyone to see it; the drawing itself was the fun.

qa.q: What did Raghav do that helped, and what could he do next time?
qa.a: He let Arnab keep going; next time he could just sit nearby without suggesting photos or praise.

qa.q: How might Arnab's mother feel if she saw the drawing later?
qa.a: She might feel delighted and surprised to find such a big, happy drawing made with no one asking for it.

grounding: The passage shows a young child drawing for nearly an hour during festival holidays with no audience, stopping when he feels done.

“Devika, it's so hot. Come under the fan,” Mumma called. It was mid-May, the cooler humming.
“I'm drawing.”
“Who is it for? For Nani?”
“It's for nobody.”
“Nobody?” Sharmila laughed. “Then why so many colours?”
“Because.” Devika pressed hard with the orange. “It's a mango tree. Now it has a swing. Now a parrot.”
Later: “Mumma, the parrot has a baby.”
Later still: “Now it's raining on the mango tree.”
Almost an hour later, Devika sat back. “Finished.”
“Can I put it on the fridge? 😊”
Devika shrugged and ran off to the cooler. The drawing stayed on the floor.

qa.q: What did Devika draw first?
qa.a: She drew a mango tree, and then added a swing and a parrot.

qa.q: What does Devika's shrug about the fridge suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt happy and finished already; she enjoyed drawing for itself and didn't care about showing it.

qa.q: How could Sharmila support this kind of play?
qa.a: By letting Devika draw as long as she wants and not turning it into a gift or display each time.

qa.q: How does Sharmila seem to see the drawing compared with Devika?
qa.a: Sharmila thinks of an audience, like Nani or the fridge, while Devika is interested only in the fun of making it.

grounding: The dialogue shows a young child drawing for nearly an hour in summer heat for nobody, stopping when she feels finished.

subtype: Reward replacing interest [Actor]
passage:
Alejandro used to read long adventure books about ships and castles, under the blanket with a torch, in their flat in Seville.
Then the library started a summer challenge: one sticker for every book finished, and a prize for twenty stickers.
By the second week Alejandro was racing. He chose thin books with big letters. Picture books meant for his little sister Rosa. Four in one afternoon.
“You didn't finish the pirate one,” Rosa said, pointing at the thick book on the shelf.
“It takes too long. It's only one sticker.”
He got his twenty stickers and a shiny medal. At home, he put it on the shelf and sat on the bed. He didn't feel like reading anything. The torch stayed in the drawer.

qa.q: What did the library give for every book finished?
qa.a: One sticker for every book, and a prize for twenty stickers.

qa.q: Why did the pirate book suddenly seem not worth it to Alejandro?
qa.a: He was excited about collecting stickers and impatient with long books that earned only one, so the reward felt more important than the story.

qa.q: What could the library or his family try instead?
qa.a: Reward time spent reading or talk about favourite stories, so the pleasure of the book stays the main thing.

qa.q: How might Rosa see her brother's new reading?
qa.a: Rosa may be puzzled to see him reading her picture books instead of his pirate stories.

grounding: The passage shows a child who loved reading choosing thin books for stickers, and his joy in reading fading as the reward took over.

passage:
The school library had a new chart: “Read and Win!” Each book returned earned one point, and ten points meant a free canteen coupon.
Deepak had always been the boy who read the whole science encyclopedia. Now he stood at the counter with five thin comics.
His friend Samir raised an eyebrow. “You finished the space book?”
“No. Too many pages. Comics are faster.”
By the end of the month Deepak had thirty points and three coupons. But when the librarian put a new book on black holes on the display, the one he would once have grabbed first, he walked past it.
“Aren't you taking that?” Samir asked.
Deepak shrugged. “It's only one point.”
Later, he felt a strange, flat feeling he couldn't name.

qa.q: What did ten points earn in the library challenge?
qa.a: Ten points earned a free canteen coupon.

qa.q: Why did Deepak walk past the new book on black holes?
qa.a: He was focused on points, and a long book was worth only one, so the prize crowded out his old interest and left him feeling flat.

qa.q: What could the librarian change to protect children's interest?
qa.a: Give points for time spent or for sharing what they learned, so long, interesting books aren't punished.

qa.q: How might Samir feel watching his friend walk past the space book?
qa.a: Samir might feel surprised and a little sad, remembering how much Deepak used to love such books.

grounding: The passage shows a child who loved reading switching to thin books for points and losing interest in the kind of books he once enjoyed.

passage:
Before: In June, Pema spent every evening in the window seat with a fat book about a girl who sails around the world. She read slowly, sometimes reading a good page twice.
During: In July, Gargi Masi said, “I'll give you twenty rupees for every book you finish.” Pema's eyes went wide. Next day she took six thin books from the school library. She finished them all by Sunday. The sailing book stayed with its bookmark on chapter nine.
After: By late August, Pema had a tin full of coins. One rainy evening Masi asked, “Why not read your sailing book?” Pema shrugged. “It's so long. And I don't really feel like reading.”
She sat by the window, the tin in her lap, watching the rain.

qa.q: On which chapter was the bookmark in the sailing book?
qa.a: The bookmark stayed on chapter nine.

qa.q: How did Pema feel about reading by late August?
qa.a: She seemed bored and flat about reading; the coins had become the point, and the old joy had faded.

qa.q: What could Gargi Masi try now to bring back Pema's love of reading?
qa.a: Stop paying per book and instead read the sailing book with Pema, talking about the story, so interest leads again.

qa.q: What might Gargi Masi realise when Pema says she doesn't feel like reading?
qa.a: Masi might feel sorry and surprised, realising the reward she meant kindly pushed out Pema's own interest.

grounding: The three beats show a child who loved reading being paid per book, choosing thin ones, and losing her original joy.

passage:
In Class 10, I was known as the one who always came first. I'm Ishita, and I learned every chapter the way you pack a suitcase: only what the exam needs.
I highlighted the likely questions from past papers and skipped the “extra reading” boxes. My parents framed my report cards. That approval felt like oxygen.
My cousin Chetan was the opposite. His marks were average, but he'd spend a whole Sunday trying to make a lemon battery work, just because.
In Class 11, we had a surprise class discussion on photosynthesis. I had scored full marks in that chapter a year earlier. I couldn't explain a single step. Chetan, visiting, explained it to me at dinner using the leaves in our pot.
I felt ashamed, and then curious for the first time in years. What else had I learned and lost?

qa.q: What did Chetan try to make work on a Sunday?
qa.a: He tried to make a lemon battery work.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when Chetan explained photosynthesis at dinner?
qa.a: Ishita felt ashamed at forgetting a chapter once scored perfectly, and then, for the first time in years, curious.

qa.q: What could Ishita try in Class 11 to learn differently?
qa.a: Reading the extra boxes and trying small experiments like Chetan's, studying to understand rather than only for marks.

qa.q: How might Ishita's parents see this change?
qa.a: They might worry about marks at first, but could come to value that Ishita is finally interested in learning.

grounding: The reflection shows a teenager who studied only for rank and approval forgetting what was crammed, and a curious cousin who kept learning.

Class teacher's note, Class 9A, parent meeting prep.
Arohi is ranked first again this term. Her mother, Mrs Urmila Joshi, will attend on Saturday.
Observations: Arohi asks me almost every week, “Will this be in the exam?” If the answer is no, she closes her notebook. She has memorised the definitions list word for word. Yet in last week's surprise quiz on last term's topics, she scored lower than half the class and looked shaken.
When we did the pond-water microscope activity, several students were thrilled. Arohi asked whether it was graded, and when I said no, she sat back and waited.
I believe the pressure of rank is producing marks but not curiosity, and she seems anxious rather than interested.
What I plan to do: I will share this gently with Mrs Joshi, show her the quiz, and suggest they talk about one topic Arohi enjoys, without marks. I'll also give Arohi a small ungraded project she chooses herself.

qa.q: What does Arohi ask the teacher almost every week?
qa.a: She asks, “Will this be in the exam?”

qa.q: Why might Arohi sit back when an activity isn't graded?
qa.a: She seems anxious and driven by rank and approval, so work without marks feels pointless to her.

qa.q: What does the teacher plan, and why could it help?
qa.a: Sharing the pattern with Mrs Joshi and giving Arohi an ungraded project she chooses, to let interest grow without pressure.

qa.q: How might Mrs Urmila Joshi react to the note?
qa.a: She may feel surprised and a bit defensive, since Arohi is first, but could also feel concerned when she sees the quiz.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a teenager working for rank and approval, cramming for tests and forgetting quickly, with little curiosity.

Tuesday.
Got 96 in chemistry. Papa smiled. That's the whole reason, honestly. I study for that smile and for my rank, nothing else.
I learnt the full chapter on acids last week in two nights. Today Asif asked me in the bus why lemon juice stops cut apples going brown. I opened my mouth and... nothing. I had written 'antioxidant' in the exam. I got the marks. I have no idea what it means.
Asif got 71 but he talked about it for ten minutes, excited, like it was a film.
I felt jealous, and not of his marks.
I don't remember anything from Class 9 either. It's like I pour it in, pour it out on the paper and the cup is empty again.
Tomorrow I'm going to ask Ma'am one question that won't be in the exam. Just to see what that feels like.
— Shreya

qa.a: Shreya got 96 in chemistry.

qa.a: Shreya felt envious of Asif's excitement and real understanding, which marks alone hadn't given Shreya.

qa.a: Asking the teacher a question that won't be in the exam, which lets curiosity lead rather than marks.
